title: Network+ Study Lab
subtitle: CompTIA Network+ N10-009 practice bank (322 questions)
note: Original practice questions with terminal labs and simulations. Not affiliated with CompTIA. Check the official N10-009 objectives before you book.

learn.idea: The OSI model splits network communication into seven layers. Each layer does one job and talks to the same layer on the other device. Knowing the layer tells you which device, protocol or problem you are dealing with.
points: Layers from bottom to top: 1 Physical, 2 Data Link, 3 Network, 4 Transport, 5 Session, 6 Presentation, 7 Application.
Data units: bits at Layer 1, frames at Layer 2, packets at Layer 3, segments (TCP) or datagrams (UDP) at Layer 4.
Layer 2 uses MAC addresses and switches. Layer 3 uses IP addresses and routers.
TCP is connection-oriented with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). UDP is connectionless and has no delivery guarantee.
Encapsulation adds a header at each layer on the way down. De-encapsulation strips them on the way up.
Hubs and cables work at Layer 1. Bridges and switches at Layer 2. Routers and Layer 3 switches at Layer 3. Load balancers and next-gen firewalls can work up to Layer 7.
learn.memory: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away (Physical to Application).

cards.front: Which OSI layer uses MAC addresses?
Which OSI layer uses IP addresses?
Layer where TLS encryption is usually placed in the OSI model?

questions.q: At which OSI layer does a router make forwarding decisions?
questions.explain: Routers read the destination IP address, which is a Layer 3 (Network) address.

questions.q: A technician finds a damaged patch cable. Which OSI layer is the problem at?
questions.explain: Cables, connectors and signals are Layer 1, the Physical layer.

questions.q: Which protocol data unit is used at the Data Link layer?
questions.explain: Layer 2 wraps packets in frames that carry source and destination MAC addresses.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for end-to-end delivery, ports and flow control?
questions.explain: Layer 4 handles ports, segmentation, flow control and, with TCP, reliable delivery.

questions.q: Which layer sets up, manages and tears down sessions between applications?
questions.explain: Layer 5, Session, controls the dialogue between two applications.

questions.q: Data is being translated, compressed or encrypted so the receiving application can read it. Which OSI layer is this?
questions.explain: Layer 6 handles formatting, compression and encryption.

questions.q: Which statement about UDP is correct?
options: It is connectionless and does not confirm delivery
questions.explain: UDP sends datagrams with no handshake and no acknowledgements. That makes it fast and suits voice, video and DNS queries.

questions.q: A standard Layer 2 switch forwards traffic based on which value?
questions.explain: A switch learns MAC addresses per port and forwards frames to the port that owns the destination MAC.

questions.q: Which device works only at Layer 1 and repeats every signal out of every port?
questions.explain: A hub has no intelligence. It repeats bits out of all ports, which creates one big collision domain.

questions.q: A web application firewall that inspects HTTP requests is working at Layer 7.
questions.explain: Inspecting HTTP content means reading application data, which is Layer 7.

questions.q: Encapsulation removes headers as data moves down the OSI stack.
questions.explain: Encapsulation adds headers on the way down. Headers are removed on the way up, which is de-encapsulation.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put the OSI layers in order from Layer 1 to Layer 7.
questions.explain: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Remember: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.

questions.q: Put the TCP three-way handshake in order.
questions.explain: SYN opens the request, SYN-ACK accepts it, ACK confirms, then data moves.

questions.q: Match each device to the OSI layer it mainly works at.
questions.explain: Hubs repeat bits (L1), switches use MACs (L2), routers use IPs (L3) and a WAF reads application traffic (L7).

learn.idea: Ports let one IP address run many services at once. The exam expects you to know the well-known ports, whether each uses TCP or UDP, and the secure version that replaces each plain-text protocol.
points: FTP 20/21, SSH and SFTP 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, DHCP 67/68, TFTP 69, HTTP 80, NTP 123, SNMP 161/162, LDAP 389, HTTPS 443, SMB 445, Syslog 514.
SMTPS 587 (submission with STARTTLS) or 465, LDAPS 636, IMAP 143 and IMAPS 993, POP3 110 and POP3S 995, SQL Server 1433, RDP 3389, SIP 5060/5061.
Plain-text protocols to replace: Telnet with SSH, HTTP with HTTPS, FTP with SFTP or FTPS, LDAP with LDAPS, SNMPv1/v2c with SNMPv3.
DNS uses UDP 53 for most queries and TCP 53 for zone transfers and large replies.
Port ranges: well-known 0 to 1023, registered 1024 to 49151, dynamic or ephemeral 49152 to 65535.
ICMP has no ports. It carries ping (echo request and reply) and error messages such as destination unreachable and TTL exceeded.
learn.memory: Telnet is 23 and talks in clear text. SSH is 22 and keeps secrets.

questions.q: Which port must be open for a remote admin to use Remote Desktop Protocol?
questions.explain: RDP listens on TCP 3389 by default.

questions.q: A firewall rule allows TCP 22. Which two services can use it?
questions.explain: SFTP runs inside SSH, so both use TCP 22. Telnet is 23 and FTPS uses 989/990 or 21 with TLS.

questions.q: Which protocol uses UDP 69 and has no authentication, so it is often used to load switch configs and firmware?
questions.explain: TFTP is a tiny file transfer protocol on UDP 69 with no login.

questions.q: Network monitoring software polls switches over which port?
questions.explain: SNMP managers poll agents on UDP 161. Agents send traps to the manager on UDP 162.

questions.q: A company wants directory lookups to be encrypted. Which port should the LDAP clients use?
questions.explain: LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) uses TCP 636. Plain LDAP uses 389.

questions.q: Which port does Syslog use by default?
questions.explain: Syslog traditionally sends messages on UDP 514. Syslog over TLS commonly uses TCP 6514.

questions.q: Which port does Microsoft SQL Server listen on by default?
questions.explain: SQL Server uses TCP 1433. 3306 is MySQL, 1521 Oracle, 5432 PostgreSQL.

questions.q: A user can send email but a firewall blocks mail clients from downloading it with the secure IMAP protocol. Which port must be opened?
questions.explain: IMAPS uses TCP 993. 143 is plain IMAP and 995 is POP3S.

questions.q: Which protocol uses port 123 to keep device clocks in sync?
questions.explain: NTP uses UDP 123. Accurate time matters for logs, Kerberos and certificates.

questions.q: VoIP phones register and set up calls using SIP. Which ports are used?
questions.explain: SIP uses 5060 for plain signalling and 5061 for SIP over TLS.

questions.q: Which range holds the ephemeral ports a client picks for its side of a connection?
questions.explain: Dynamic or ephemeral ports run from 49152 to 65535. Port numbers stop at 65535.

questions.q: DNS zone transfers between DNS servers use TCP port 53.
questions.explain: Normal queries use UDP 53, but zone transfers and large answers use TCP 53.

questions.q: ICMP uses port 7 for ping.
questions.explain: ICMP is its own protocol and has no ports. Ping uses ICMP echo request and echo reply.

questions.q: Match the insecure protocol with its secure replacement.
questions.explain: Each replacement adds encryption, authentication or both.

questions.q: Match the port to the service.
questions.explain: These are among the most tested port numbers on Network+.

questions.q: Which port is used for email submission from a client to a mail server with STARTTLS?
questions.explain: Port 587 is the submission port. Clients log in and upgrade to TLS with STARTTLS. Port 25 is server-to-server relay.

learn.idea: An IPv4 address is 32 bits. The subnet mask, written in CIDR as /24 and so on, says how many bits are the network and how many are hosts. Subnetting splits one network into smaller ones.
points: Usable hosts per subnet = 2 to the power of host bits, minus 2. The first address is the network ID and the last is the broadcast.
169.254.0.0/16 is APIPA. A host gives itself one when it cannot reach a DHCP server.
127.0.0.0/8 is loopback. 100.64.0.0/10 is carrier-grade NAT space.
Block size = 256 minus the interesting octet of the mask. A /26 has blocks of 64: .0, .64, .128, .192.
VLSM lets you use different mask sizes inside one network so you waste fewer addresses. A /31 is used on point-to-point links.
learn.memory: Hosts = 2^h - 2. Subnets jump in blocks of 256 minus the mask.

cards.front: Smallest subnet for a point-to-point link?

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a /27 subnet provide?
questions.explain: A /27 leaves 5 host bits. 2^5 = 32, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 30.

questions.q: How many usable hosts are in a /22 network?
questions.explain: A /22 leaves 10 host bits. 2^10 = 1024, minus 2 = 1022.

questions.q: A network admin borrows 3 bits from a /24 to make subnets. How many subnets does this create?
questions.explain: Subnets = 2^borrowed bits. 2^3 = 8 subnets, each a /27.

questions.q: What is the broadcast address of 192.168.10.64/26?
questions.explain: A /26 has blocks of 64. The subnet starting at .64 runs to .127, so .127 is the broadcast.

questions.q: Which subnet does host 10.1.1.200/27 belong to?
questions.explain: A /27 has blocks of 32: .160, .192, .224. 200 falls in the block that starts at .192.

questions.q: Which subnet mask is a /28?
questions.explain: 28 bits means 255.255.255 plus 4 more bits in the last octet: 128+64+32+16 = 240.

questions.q: An office needs one subnet for 50 hosts and wants to waste as few addresses as possible. Which mask should be used?
questions.explain: A /26 gives 62 usable hosts, the smallest size that fits 50. A /27 only gives 30.

questions.q: A workstation shows the IP 169.254.33.10. What is the most likely cause?
options: It could not reach a DHCP server
It has a static IP set
It is on the guest VLAN
questions.explain: 169.254.x.x is APIPA. Windows assigns it when no DHCP offer arrives.

questions.q: Which address is a private RFC 1918 address?
questions.explain: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 is private. 172.32.x.x is public.

questions.q: Which mask is best for a WAN link between two routers that only needs two addresses?
questions.explain: A /30 has exactly 2 usable addresses. Some routers also support /31 for point-to-point links.

questions.q: Which address range is reserved for carrier-grade NAT between an ISP and its customers?
questions.explain: RFC 6598 sets aside 100.64.0.0/10 for carrier-grade NAT, so it does not clash with customer private ranges.

questions.q: Which statement describes VLSM?
options: Using subnets of different sizes inside the same network
Giving every subnet the same mask
Assigning IPs from a DHCP pool
questions.explain: Variable length subnet masking lets you size each subnet to its need, such as /30 for links and /24 for user LANs.

questions.q: The first address in a subnet is the network ID and cannot be given to a host.
questions.explain: The network ID identifies the subnet itself. The last address is the broadcast.

questions.q: 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 is used for multicast.
questions.explain: That is the old Class D range, now written 224.0.0.0/4, reserved for multicast groups.

questions.q: How many usable host addresses does a 255.255.255.248 mask allow?
questions.explain: 248 is a /29, which leaves 3 host bits. 2^3 = 8, minus 2 = 6.

questions.q: A host is 192.168.5.130 with mask 255.255.255.128. Which is a valid default gateway on the same subnet?
questions.explain: The subnet is 192.168.5.128/25 with hosts .129 to .254. Only .129 is in that range.

questions.q: Match the CIDR prefix to its usable hosts.
questions.explain: Each extra mask bit halves the host count. Subtract 2 for network and broadcast.

questions.q: A company is given 192.168.50.0/24 and splits it into /28 subnets. How many subnets does it get?
questions.explain: Going from /24 to /28 borrows 4 bits. 2^4 = 16 subnets of 14 hosts each.

learn.idea: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses written in hex. It has no broadcast and uses multicast and neighbor discovery instead of ARP. Traffic can be unicast, multicast, anycast or broadcast.
points: Shorten IPv6 by dropping leading zeros in each group and replacing one run of all-zero groups with ::. You can only use :: once.
Address types: global unicast 2000::/3, unique local fc00::/7 (fd00::/8 in practice), link-local fe80::/10, multicast ff00::/8, loopback ::1.
SLAAC lets a host build its own address from the router's prefix. EUI-64 uses the MAC address to make the interface ID.
Neighbor Discovery Protocol (NDP) replaces ARP and uses ICMPv6 messages.
Transition methods: dual stack (run both), tunneling (6to4, Teredo) and NAT64 translation.
Unicast is one to one. Multicast is one to a group. Anycast goes to the nearest of many. Broadcast is one to all in IPv4 only.
learn.memory: IPv6 never shouts. It has no broadcast, only multicast.

cards.front: How many times can :: be used in one address?

cards.back: Delivered to the nearest of several hosts with the same address.

questions.q: Which is the correct shortened form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329?
questions.explain: Drop leading zeros in each group and replace the run of three zero groups with :: once.

questions.q: A host has the address fe80::1c2a:3fff:fe4b:12. What type of address is this?
questions.explain: fe80::/10 is link-local. It only works on the local segment and every IPv6 interface has one.

questions.q: Which IPv6 feature lets a host build its own global address from the router advertisement prefix without a DHCP server?
questions.explain: Stateless address autoconfiguration uses the prefix from the router advertisement.

questions.q: Which protocol does IPv6 use instead of ARP to find MAC addresses?
questions.explain: Neighbor Discovery Protocol uses ICMPv6 neighbor solicitation and advertisement messages.

questions.q: A company runs IPv4 and IPv6 on every device at the same time while it migrates. What is this called?
questions.explain: Dual stack runs both protocols side by side. It is the most common transition method.

questions.q: Which traffic type sends a packet to the closest of several servers that share the same address?
questions.explain: Anycast routing delivers to the nearest node. Public DNS resolvers use it a lot.

questions.q: A video stream must reach a group of subscribed hosts without sending a copy to everyone. Which traffic type fits?
questions.explain: Multicast sends one stream to hosts that joined the group. IGMP manages group membership in IPv4.

questions.q: IPv6 supports broadcast addresses for sending to every host on a link.
questions.explain: IPv6 has no broadcast. It uses multicast groups such as ff02::1 (all nodes) instead.

questions.q: EUI-64 builds the interface ID from the device's MAC address.
questions.explain: EUI-64 splits the 48-bit MAC, inserts fffe in the middle and flips the seventh bit.

questions.q: Match the IPv6 prefix to its type.
questions.explain: Global unicast is routable on the internet, link-local stays on the segment, unique local is like private IPv4, and ff marks multicast.

learn.idea: Networks are built from physical and virtual appliances, laid out in a topology, and more and more run in the cloud. The exam asks which device or design fits a need.
points: Firewalls filter traffic. A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds application awareness and IPS. IDS detects and alerts. IPS sits inline and blocks.
Load balancers spread traffic across servers. Proxies make requests for clients. A content delivery network (CDN) caches content near users.
Topologies: star (hub and spoke), mesh (full or partial), bus, ring, hybrid. Data centres use spine and leaf. The three-tier model is core, distribution, access.
North-south traffic enters or leaves the data centre. East-west traffic moves between servers inside it.
Cloud models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS. Deployment: public, private, hybrid, community. A VPC is your private network inside a public cloud.
SDN separates the control plane from the data plane. SD-WAN manages several WAN links from a central controller. NFV runs network functions as virtual machines.
Cloud gateways: an internet gateway gives a VPC internet access. A NAT gateway lets private subnets reach out without being reachable from outside.
learn.memory: IDS tells. IPS stops.

cards.back: IDS detects and alerts. IPS is inline and blocks.
Every leaf switch connects to every spine switch. Used in data centres.
Server to server inside the data centre.
The control plane from the data plane.
Lets private subnets reach the internet without inbound access.

questions.q: Which device sits inline and can drop malicious traffic as it passes?
questions.explain: An intrusion prevention system is placed in the traffic path so it can block. An IDS only watches a copy and alerts.

questions.q: A web site needs traffic spread across four identical web servers, with failed servers taken out of rotation. Which device should be used?
questions.explain: Load balancers distribute requests and use health checks to skip failed servers.

questions.q: Which data centre design connects every access switch to every aggregation switch so any server is the same number of hops from any other?
questions.explain: In spine and leaf every leaf links to every spine, which gives predictable latency for east-west traffic.

questions.q: A company pays for virtual machines, storage and networks but manages the OS and apps itself. Which cloud model is this?
questions.explain: Infrastructure as a Service gives you the building blocks. You manage the OS upwards.

questions.q: Developers want to upload code and let the provider handle servers, OS patching and runtime. Which cloud model fits?
questions.explain: Platform as a Service hosts your code on a managed platform.

questions.q: Which technology manages several branch internet and MPLS links from a central controller and steers traffic by application?
questions.explain: SD-WAN builds an overlay across many WAN links and picks the best path per application.

questions.q: Private servers in a cloud VPC need to download patches but must not be reachable from the internet. What should be added?
questions.explain: A NAT gateway allows outbound connections from private subnets and blocks unsolicited inbound connections.

questions.q: Which topology gives the most redundancy because every node has a link to every other node?
questions.explain: A full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links. It is very resilient but costly.

questions.q: Traffic moving between two application servers inside the same data centre is called what?
questions.explain: East-west is lateral traffic inside the data centre. North-south crosses the edge.

questions.q: Which service caches web content on servers close to users around the world to cut load times?
questions.explain: A content delivery network stores copies at edge locations near users.

questions.q: A next-generation firewall can identify applications such as Facebook or BitTorrent even when they use port 443.
questions.explain: NGFWs use deep packet inspection and application signatures rather than port numbers alone.

questions.q: In SDN the data plane decides where traffic should go and the control plane forwards the packets.
questions.explain: It is the other way round. The control plane decides, and the data plane forwards.

questions.q: Match the cloud term to its meaning.
pairs: Shared provider infrastructure open to anyone who pays
Mix of private and public that work together
Shared by organisations with common needs
questions.explain: Deployment models describe who owns and shares the infrastructure.

questions.q: Which three-tier layer connects end user devices such as PCs and phones?
questions.explain: The access layer is where users plug in. Distribution aggregates access switches and core is the fast backbone.

questions.q: Match each network function virtualisation term to its description.
pairs: Network functions such as firewalls run as virtual machines
Isolated private network in a public cloud
Stateful virtual firewall rules on a cloud instance
questions.explain: These are the virtual building blocks used in cloud and data centre networks.

questions.q: Which statement about a forward proxy is correct?
options: It makes requests to the internet on behalf of internal clients
It sits in front of web servers and hides them from users
questions.explain: A forward proxy acts for clients. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers.

learn.idea: Copper and fibre carry the signals. Each cable type has a speed and a distance limit, and each needs the right connector or transceiver.
points: Twisted pair categories: Cat 5e 1 Gbps, Cat 6 10 Gbps up to 55 m, Cat 6a 10 Gbps to 100 m, Cat 8 25/40 Gbps to 30 m. Standard copper runs are 100 m.
Single-mode fibre has a small core, uses lasers and goes many kilometres. Multimode has a larger core, uses LEDs or VCSELs and goes a few hundred metres.
Fibre connectors: LC (small, common in SFPs), SC (square, push-pull), ST (round, twist lock), MPO (many fibres in one).
Transceivers: SFP (1 Gbps), SFP+ (10 Gbps), QSFP+ (40 Gbps), QSFP28 (100 Gbps). A bidirectional (BiDi) optic uses two wavelengths on one strand.
Coax uses F-type or BNC connectors. RG-6 is used for cable broadband.
Plenum cable has fire-resistant jacketing for air-handling spaces. PVC is not allowed there.
T568A and T568B are wiring standards. A straight-through cable has the same standard on both ends. A crossover has A on one end and B on the other.
learn.memory: Single-mode is for long, skinny distances. Multimode is for short, fat cores.

cards.front: Max length for a twisted pair run?
Fibre for long campus or metro links?

cards.back: T568A on one end, T568B on the other.

questions.q: A link must run 8 km between two buildings. Which media should be used?
questions.explain: Single-mode fibre carries laser light over many kilometres. Multimode tops out at a few hundred metres.

questions.q: Which cable category supports 10 Gbps over the full 100 m?
questions.explain: Cat 6a is rated for 10GBASE-T at 100 m. Cat 6 only reaches about 55 m at 10 Gbps.

questions.q: A technician must install network cable above a drop ceiling used for air return. Which jacket is required?
questions.explain: Plenum-rated cable gives off less toxic smoke and slows flames in air-handling spaces. Fire codes require it.

questions.q: Which transceiver is used for 10 Gbps fibre or DAC connections on most switches?
questions.explain: SFP+ is the 10 Gbps version of the small form-factor pluggable.

questions.q: Which fibre connector is small, has a latch and is used on most SFP modules?
questions.explain: The LC (Lucent connector) is the small form-factor connector found on SFPs.

questions.q: Which connector is used on RG-6 coax for cable internet?
questions.explain: F-type screws onto coax for cable modems and TV.

questions.q: Two switches in the same rack need a cheap 10 Gbps link of about 3 m. Which option is best?
questions.explain: A DAC is a twinax cable with SFP+ ends built in. It is cheap and ideal for short in-rack links.

questions.q: A data centre wants to use one fibre strand for both transmit and receive. Which optic does this?
questions.explain: BiDi optics send and receive on different wavelengths over a single strand.

questions.q: Multimode fibre has a larger core than single-mode fibre.
questions.explain: Multimode cores are 50 or 62.5 microns. Single-mode cores are about 9 microns.

questions.q: A Cat 6 cable can be run 150 m between a switch and a desk as long as it is shielded.
questions.explain: Twisted pair Ethernet is limited to 100 m whether shielded or not. Longer runs need a switch, extender or fibre.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put the T568B pin colours in order from pin 1 to pin 8.
questions.explain: T568B: white-orange, orange, white-green, blue, white-blue, green, white-brown, brown.

questions.q: Match the transceiver to its usual speed.
questions.explain: Each newer form factor raises the speed. QSFP packs four lanes.

questions.q: Which cable is wired T568A on one end and T568B on the other?
questions.explain: Crossover swaps the transmit and receive pairs. Modern ports with auto MDI-X rarely need it.

questions.q: A technician needs to connect a laptop to a switch console port. Which cable is used?
questions.explain: A console or rollover cable connects to the switch console port, often through a USB-to-serial adapter.

learn.idea: Routers move packets between networks using a routing table. Routes come from directly connected interfaces, static entries or dynamic routing protocols. NAT and PAT let many private hosts share public addresses.
points: Static routes are typed in by hand. A default route (0.0.0.0/0) catches everything with no better match.
The router picks the longest prefix match first. If two sources offer the same prefix, the lower administrative distance wins.
Administrative distance: connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120, iBGP 200.
OSPF is a link-state interior protocol that uses cost. EIGRP is an advanced distance-vector protocol. RIP uses hop count with a limit of 15. BGP is the path-vector protocol of the internet.
NAT translates private to public addresses. PAT (NAT overload) maps many hosts to one public IP using port numbers.
First hop redundancy protocols such as VRRP and HSRP share a virtual gateway IP between two routers so hosts keep working if one fails.
Subinterfaces on one router port can route between VLANs. This is called router on a stick.
learn.memory: Longest match first, then lowest AD, then lowest metric.

cards.front: Protocol used between ISPs on the internet?

cards.back: Many private hosts share one public IP using ports.
A shared virtual default gateway for redundancy.

questions.q: A router has routes to 10.0.0.0/8, 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.1.0/24. Which route is used for a packet to 10.1.1.50?
questions.explain: The router always picks the most specific (longest) prefix that matches.

questions.q: A router learns 172.16.5.0/24 from both OSPF and EIGRP. Which route goes in the routing table?
options: EIGRP, because its administrative distance is 90
OSPF, because its administrative distance is 110
questions.explain: With the same prefix the lowest administrative distance wins. EIGRP is 90 and OSPF is 110.

questions.q: Which routing protocol is used to exchange routes between different autonomous systems on the internet?
questions.explain: BGP is the exterior gateway protocol that connects ISPs and large networks.

questions.q: Which dynamic routing protocol is link-state and uses cost based on bandwidth?
questions.explain: OSPF builds a full map of the area and runs the SPF algorithm using interface cost.

questions.q: A small office has 40 PCs and one public IP from the ISP. What lets all PCs reach the internet at once?
questions.explain: Port address translation maps each inside connection to a unique port on the one public IP.

questions.q: A web server on a private address must be reachable from the internet at a fixed public IP. What should be configured?
questions.explain: Static NAT or a port forward maps a public address and port to the inside server every time.

questions.q: Two routers share the virtual IP 192.168.1.1. If the active router fails, the standby takes over. Which protocol is this?
questions.explain: VRRP (and Cisco's HSRP) provide a shared virtual default gateway.

questions.q: What does the route 0.0.0.0/0 represent?
questions.explain: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination. It is used when no more specific route exists.

questions.q: Which protocol has a maximum hop count of 15?
questions.explain: RIP counts hops and treats 16 as unreachable, which limits it to small networks.

questions.q: Router on a stick uses subinterfaces on one physical port to route between VLANs over a trunk.
questions.explain: Each subinterface is tagged for one VLAN and acts as that VLAN's gateway.

questions.q: A static route has a higher administrative distance than OSPF by default.
questions.explain: Static routes have an AD of 1, which is lower and more trusted than OSPF at 110.

questions.q: Match the route source to its default administrative distance.
questions.explain: Lower AD means the source is more trusted.

questions.q: Which statement about a Layer 3 switch is correct?
options: It can route between VLANs using switch virtual interfaces
It needs an external router for every VLAN
questions.explain: A Layer 3 switch uses SVIs as gateways and routes in hardware.

questions.q: An engineer types 'show ip route' and sees an entry marked 'S*'. What is it?
questions.explain: S means static and the asterisk marks the candidate default route.

learn.idea: Switches connect devices inside a LAN. VLANs split one switch into separate broadcast domains, trunks carry many VLANs between switches, and spanning tree stops loops.
points: A switch builds a MAC address table by reading source MACs. Unknown destinations are flooded out of every port in the VLAN.
Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain and IP subnet. Traffic between VLANs needs a router or Layer 3 switch.
Access ports carry one VLAN. Trunk ports carry many VLANs using 802.1Q tags. The native VLAN is sent untagged on a trunk.
A voice VLAN lets an IP phone and a PC share one port while their traffic stays separate.
Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1D) elects a root bridge (lowest bridge ID) and blocks redundant paths. RSTP (802.1w) converges faster.
Link aggregation (LACP, 802.3ad) bundles several ports into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy.
Jumbo frames raise the MTU above 1500 bytes, usually to 9000, for storage and data centre traffic. Every device in the path must match.
learn.memory: Access = one VLAN. Trunk = many VLANs, tagged.

cards.back: VLAN sent untagged on an 802.1Q trunk.

questions.q: Which standard adds VLAN tags to frames on a trunk link?
questions.explain: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag that names the VLAN.

questions.q: A switch receives a frame for a MAC address that is not in its table. What does it do?
options: Floods it out of every port in that VLAN except the one it came in on
Sends it to the default gateway
questions.explain: Unknown unicast frames are flooded so the frame reaches the destination. The reply then teaches the switch where it lives.

questions.q: Users report the network slowing to a crawl right after someone plugged both ends of a patch cable into the same switch. What should have prevented this?
questions.explain: The cable made a Layer 2 loop and a broadcast storm. STP detects and blocks loops.

questions.q: How is the STP root bridge chosen?
questions.explain: The bridge ID is the priority plus the MAC address. Lowest wins, so admins lower the priority on the switch they want as root.

questions.q: An IP phone and a PC share one switch port. Which feature keeps phone traffic in its own VLAN?
questions.explain: The voice VLAN tags phone traffic while the PC's traffic stays in the data VLAN.

questions.q: A server needs 4 Gbps of bandwidth to a switch and should keep working if one cable fails. What should be used?
options: LACP link aggregation of four 1 Gbps ports
questions.explain: LACP bundles ports into one logical link that shares load and survives a member link failure.

questions.q: Storage traffic in the data centre would benefit from larger frames. What should be configured end to end?
questions.explain: Jumbo frames cut overhead for large transfers. Every switch and host on the path must use the same MTU.

questions.q: Hosts in VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 on the same switch cannot reach each other. What is needed?
options: A router or Layer 3 switch to route between the VLANs
questions.explain: Each VLAN is a separate subnet. Moving between them requires routing.

questions.q: Which STP port state forwards frames and learns MAC addresses?
questions.explain: Only the forwarding state passes user traffic. Blocking ports stop loops.

questions.q: A broadcast sent by a host in VLAN 30 reaches every port in every VLAN on the switch.
questions.explain: Broadcasts stay inside their own VLAN. That is the main point of VLANs.

questions.q: Rapid Spanning Tree (802.1w) converges faster than the original 802.1D STP.
questions.explain: RSTP uses proposal and agreement and can reconverge in seconds instead of 30 to 50 seconds.

questions.q: Match the switch feature to what it does.
pairs: Carries one VLAN to an end device
Copies traffic to a monitoring port
Bundles links into one logical link
questions.explain: These are the core switch port settings on the exam.

questions.q: A trunk between two switches carries VLAN 1 untagged and all others tagged. What is VLAN 1 here?
questions.explain: Untagged traffic on an 802.1Q trunk belongs to the native VLAN. Mismatched native VLANs cause problems.

questions.q: A network engineer wants an IDS to see all traffic on a switch uplink. What should be configured?
options: Port mirroring (SPAN) to the IDS port
A new VLAN for the IDS
questions.explain: SPAN copies frames from chosen ports or VLANs to the monitor port.

questions.q: Put the steps a switch takes when a frame arrives in order.
steps: Reads the source MAC and records it against the incoming port
Looks up the destination MAC in its table
Forwards out the matching port, or floods if unknown
Resets the age timer for that table entry when the host sends again
questions.explain: Learn the source first, then look up the destination, then forward or flood.

questions.q: Which value is checked first when spanning tree elects the root bridge?
questions.explain: Priority (default 32768) is compared first. The MAC address only breaks ties.

learn.idea: Wi-Fi uses the 802.11 standards over 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz. Good designs pick the right band, non-overlapping channels and strong encryption.
points: 802.11a 5 GHz 54 Mbps, b 2.4 GHz 11 Mbps, g 2.4 GHz 54 Mbps, n (Wi-Fi 4) 2.4/5 GHz, ac (Wi-Fi 5) 5 GHz, ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E) 2.4/5/6 GHz, be (Wi-Fi 7) adds wider channels.
In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap in the US. 5 GHz has many more channels and supports channel bonding to 40, 80 or 160 MHz.
2.4 GHz travels further and through walls better. 5 and 6 GHz are faster but shorter range.
WPA2 uses AES with CCMP. WPA3 adds SAE in place of the pre-shared key handshake and forward secrecy. WPA2/3 Enterprise uses 802.1X and RADIUS.
SSID is the network name. BSSID is the AP radio's MAC. ESSID is one SSID across many APs for roaming.
Antennas: omnidirectional covers all around, directional (Yagi, patch, parabolic) focuses in one direction for point-to-point links.
Autonomous APs are configured one by one. Lightweight APs are run by a wireless LAN controller. Captive portals show a login or terms page for guests.
learn.memory: 1, 6, 11: the only three 2.4 GHz channels that do not step on each other.

cards.front: Non-overlapping 2.4 GHz channels in the US?

cards.back: MAC address of an AP radio.
Directional, such as a Yagi or parabolic.

questions.q: An admin is setting up three APs in a hallway on 2.4 GHz. Which channels should be used?
questions.explain: In the US only 1, 6 and 11 avoid overlap in 2.4 GHz.

questions.q: Which wireless standard was the first to add the 6 GHz band?
questions.explain: Wi-Fi 6E is 802.11ax extended into the 6 GHz band.

questions.q: A company wants each employee to log on to Wi-Fi with their own directory credentials. What should be used?
options: An open SSID with MAC filtering
questions.explain: Enterprise mode sends each user's credentials to a RADIUS server through 802.1X.

questions.q: Which WPA3 feature protects a weak pre-shared key against offline dictionary attacks?
questions.explain: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals replaces the PSK four-way handshake and resists offline cracking.

questions.q: Two buildings 400 m apart need a wireless bridge. Which antenna type is best?
options: Directional, such as a parabolic or Yagi
questions.explain: Directional antennas focus energy in one direction for long point-to-point links.

questions.q: Users in a large warehouse should move between 30 APs without reconnecting. What should all APs share?
questions.explain: An extended service set uses one SSID across many APs so clients roam.

questions.q: Which device centrally manages many lightweight access points?
questions.explain: A WLAN controller pushes config, channels and power to lightweight APs.

questions.q: Hotel guests see a terms-of-use page before they can browse the internet. What is this?
questions.explain: A captive portal holds new clients on a web page until they log in or accept terms.

questions.q: Which band gives the longest range through walls?
questions.explain: Lower frequencies travel further and pass through obstacles better.

questions.q: A dense office suffers interference on 5 GHz with 80 MHz channels. What change helps most?
options: Use narrower 20 or 40 MHz channels so APs can use more non-overlapping channels
Switch every AP to 2.4 GHz channel 6
Raise every AP to full power
questions.explain: Narrower channels mean more separate channels to spread across APs, which cuts co-channel interference.

questions.q: WEP is acceptable for a new wireless deployment if a long key is used.
questions.explain: WEP is broken and can be cracked in minutes regardless of key length. Use WPA2 or WPA3.

questions.q: 802.11ac works only in the 5 GHz band.
questions.explain: Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac) is a 5 GHz standard. Dual-band APs run 802.11n on 2.4 GHz alongside it.

questions.q: Match the standard to its band.
questions.explain: Knowing the band helps you pick the right standard for range or speed.

questions.q: Match the wireless term to its meaning.
questions.explain: These terms come up in Wi-Fi design and troubleshooting.

questions.q: A wireless survey shows strong signal but poor throughput in one area. Which value should the technician check first?
questions.explain: A strong signal with high noise still gives a poor SNR, which forces lower data rates and retries.

questions.q: Which wireless authentication method sends users to a RADIUS server using a TLS tunnel and a username and password?
questions.explain: PEAP builds a TLS tunnel to protect the inner username and password exchange.

learn.idea: Equipment needs a proper home: racks, patch panels, power, cooling and labels. Power over Ethernet feeds phones, APs and cameras through the data cable.
points: PoE 802.3af gives up to 15.4 W per port, PoE+ 802.3at gives 30 W, PoE++ 802.3bt gives 60 W (Type 3) or up to 90 W (Type 4) at the switch port.
The MDF is the main distribution frame where the building connects to the outside. IDFs serve each floor or wing.
Patch panels terminate horizontal cable runs with a punchdown tool (110 block). Short patch cables connect panel ports to switch ports.
Rack units: 1U is 1.75 inches. Hot aisle and cold aisle layouts keep exhaust away from intakes.
UPS gives short battery power and clean voltage. A generator covers long outages. A PDU spreads power in the rack.
Watch temperature and humidity. High humidity causes condensation, low humidity causes static.
Fire suppression in server rooms uses clean agents such as FM-200 instead of water where possible.
learn.memory: af 15, at 30, bt 60 to 90.

cards.back: Up to 90 W at the switch port.
MDF is the main wiring point. IDFs serve floors or areas.
So hot exhaust is not pulled into equipment intakes.

questions.q: A PTZ camera needs 25 W from the switch port. Which PoE standard is the minimum?
questions.explain: 802.3af only gives 15.4 W. PoE+ gives up to 30 W.

questions.q: Which standard supports the most power per port for devices like digital signage and high-power APs?
questions.explain: 802.3bt (PoE++) Type 4 gives up to about 90 W.

questions.q: Where does the telco or ISP line usually enter a building and connect to the core equipment?
questions.explain: The main distribution frame is the central point. Intermediate frames branch out to floors.

questions.q: Which tool is used to terminate horizontal cable runs on the back of a patch panel?
questions.explain: Patch panels use 110-style IDC blocks that need a punchdown tool.

questions.q: Servers keep overheating because their intakes face the exhaust of the row in front. Which design fixes this?
questions.explain: Rows face each other so cold air feeds the fronts and hot exhaust is collected at the backs.

questions.q: Which device keeps network gear running for a few minutes during a power cut and smooths out sags and spikes?
questions.explain: An uninterruptible power supply bridges short outages and conditions power.

questions.q: A 42U rack has a 2U UPS, a 1U patch panel and three 2U servers. How much space is left?
questions.explain: 2 + 1 + 6 = 9U used. 42 minus 9 is 33U.

questions.q: Which environmental problem increases the risk of electrostatic discharge damage?
questions.explain: Dry air lets static build up. Very humid air causes condensation instead.

questions.q: Water sprinklers are the preferred fire suppression system for a server room.
questions.explain: Water destroys electronics. Clean agent systems such as FM-200 or inert gas are preferred.

questions.q: One rack unit (1U) is 1.75 inches tall.
questions.explain: Rack equipment is measured in units of 1.75 inches (44.45 mm).

questions.q: A switch has a 370 W PoE budget. How many 802.3at devices drawing the full 30 W can it power at once?
questions.explain: 370 divided by 30 is 12.3, so 12 devices at full power.

questions.q: Match the item to where it belongs.
pairs: Wiring closet that serves a floor
Point where the provider's responsibility ends
questions.explain: Physical layout terms are tested in installation questions.

questions.q: Which document shows the physical locations of racks, cable runs and wall jacks?
questions.explain: Physical diagrams show where things are. Logical diagrams show how they connect.

questions.q: Where does the internet provider's responsibility for the circuit end?
options: The patch panel in the IDF
questions.explain: The demarc is the handoff point. Problems on your side of it are yours to fix.

questions.q: Network gear in a remote closet shuts down every summer afternoon. Which monitoring should be added?
options: Temperature and humidity sensors with alerts
questions.explain: Environmental sensors warn before heat causes thermal shutdowns.

questions.q: Which statement about a generator in a data centre is correct?
options: It covers long outages while the UPS covers the gap until it starts
It replaces the need for a UPS
It conditions power better than a UPS
questions.explain: The UPS keeps power up for the seconds or minutes the generator needs to start.

learn.idea: Good records make networks easy to support. Change management stops surprise outages, and life cycle tracking tells you when gear goes out of support.
points: Physical diagrams show racks, rooms and cable runs. Logical diagrams show subnets, VLANs and routing.
Rack diagrams, cable maps, IPAM records, asset inventories and baselines are all part of documentation.
A baseline records normal performance so you can spot when something changes.
Change management: request, impact review, approval by a change advisory board, scheduled window, rollback plan, then documentation.
End of life (EOL) means the vendor stops selling. End of support (EOS) means no more patches. Plan replacements before EOS.
SLA sets the service level a provider promises. MOU is a less formal agreement. NDA protects confidential information.
Configuration management keeps a golden config and tracks changes so you can spot drift.
learn.memory: No rollback plan, no change.

cards.back: Logical shows how traffic flows. Physical shows where the gear is.
Change advisory board that approves changes.
End of support. No more patches.
When a device's settings move away from the approved baseline.

questions.q: Which diagram shows VLANs, subnets and routing between them?
questions.explain: Logical diagrams show how the network works, not where the boxes sit.

questions.q: A technician needs to know what normal CPU and bandwidth use looks like before investigating a slowdown. What should they compare against?
questions.explain: A baseline gives normal values so unusual readings stand out.

questions.q: Before a core switch upgrade, what must be written in case the change fails?
questions.explain: A rollback or backout plan explains how to return to the working state.

questions.q: Who usually approves a high-impact production change?
questions.explain: The CAB reviews risk, timing and impact before approving changes.

questions.q: A firewall model will receive no more security patches after next year. What life cycle stage is this?
questions.explain: Once a product reaches end of support it gets no fixes, which is a security risk.

questions.q: Which document defines the uptime percentage an ISP guarantees and the credit owed if it is missed?
questions.explain: A service level agreement sets measurable targets and penalties.

questions.q: A tool reports that 12 switches have settings that differ from the approved template. What is this called?
questions.explain: Drift is unplanned change from the golden configuration.

questions.q: Change management is only needed for hardware changes, not configuration changes.
questions.explain: Config changes cause many outages, so they go through change management too.

questions.q: An IPAM tool tracks which IP addresses and subnets are assigned and to what.
questions.explain: IP address management keeps subnets, DHCP scopes and DNS records in one place.

questions.q: Put a standard change management process in order.
steps: Get approval from the change board
Make the change in the maintenance window
questions.explain: Request, assess, approve, implement in the window, then verify and document.

questions.q: Match the agreement to its purpose.
pairs: Measurable service targets from a provider
Rules for how users may use systems
questions.explain: These agreements appear across Network+ and Security+.

questions.q: Which record shows the serial numbers, locations and warranty dates of all network devices?
questions.explain: The asset inventory tracks each device through its life cycle.

learn.idea: Monitoring tells you a problem is coming before users call. SNMP polls device health, syslog collects events, and flow data shows who is talking to whom.
points: SNMP managers poll agents for values stored in the MIB, each identified by an OID. Traps are alerts the agent sends without being asked.
SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption. v1 and v2c only use community strings in clear text.
Syslog severities run 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug.
NetFlow, sFlow and IPFIX record flow metadata: source, destination, ports, protocol, bytes. They show top talkers without full packet capture.
Port mirroring and taps give full packet copies for analysis with tools like Wireshark.
Interface counters to watch: CRC errors, runts, giants, input and output drops, collisions.
A SIEM collects logs from many sources, correlates them and raises alerts.
learn.memory: Every Alley Cat Eats Watermelon Nicely In Daylight (severity 0 to 7).

cards.back: Flow metadata such as IPs, ports and byte counts.
The database of values an SNMP agent exposes.
Physical layer problems such as bad cables or interference.
Collects and correlates logs from many systems.

questions.q: A switch sends an alert to the NMS the moment a port goes down, without being polled. What is this?
questions.explain: A trap is sent by the agent on its own when an event happens.

questions.q: Which SNMP version should be used to encrypt and authenticate monitoring traffic?
questions.explain: SNMPv3 adds users, authentication and privacy (encryption).

questions.q: Which syslog severity level is the most severe?
questions.explain: Lower numbers are more severe. 0 means the system is unusable.

questions.q: The security team wants to know which internal hosts sent the most data to the internet last week without storing full packets. Which tool fits?
questions.explain: Flow records hold who talked to whom and how much, without payloads.

questions.q: An interface shows a rising count of CRC errors. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: CRC errors mean frames arrived corrupted, which points to Layer 1 issues.

questions.q: Which system collects logs from firewalls, servers and switches, then correlates them to raise alerts?
questions.explain: A security information and event management system centralises and correlates events.

questions.q: In SNMP, what uniquely identifies a single value such as an interface's input octets?
questions.explain: Each value has an object identifier in the MIB tree.

questions.q: An admin sets switches to log at level 7. What will happen?
options: Every message including debug output will be logged, which can flood the server
questions.explain: Level 7 includes everything from emergency down to debug. It is useful briefly but very noisy.

questions.q: Which interface counter shows frames smaller than the 64-byte Ethernet minimum?
questions.explain: Runts are undersized frames, often caused by collisions or a bad NIC. Giants are oversized.

questions.q: SNMPv2c community strings are sent in clear text.
questions.explain: Anyone capturing the traffic can read v1 or v2c community strings, which is why v3 is preferred.

questions.q: Port mirroring sends a copy of traffic to a monitoring port without affecting the original traffic.
questions.explain: SPAN duplicates frames to the analyser port while normal forwarding continues.

questions.q: Match the syslog severity number to its name.
questions.explain: The order runs from most to least severe.

questions.q: Which tool is best for capturing and reading individual packets to see the exact TCP flags in a handshake?
questions.explain: A protocol analyser decodes each packet field by field.

questions.q: Monitoring shows an uplink at 98% use every afternoon. What should be done first to confirm the cause?
options: Check flow data for the top talkers and applications
questions.explain: Flow data shows which hosts and applications fill the link before you decide on a fix.

learn.idea: Availability is about removing single points of failure. Disaster recovery plans say how quickly systems must come back and how much data you can lose.
points: RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data loss is acceptable, measured in time. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long a restore may take.
MTTR is the mean time to repair. MTBF is the mean time between failures.
Hot sites are ready to run now. Warm sites have hardware but need data and setup. Cold sites are an empty room with power.
Active-active means both systems carry traffic. Active-passive means one waits on standby.
Redundancy tools: dual power supplies, NIC teaming, LACP, FHRP, multiple ISPs, clustering.
Test DR plans with tabletop exercises, failover tests and validation tests.
Backups: full, incremental (changes since the last backup), differential (changes since the last full).
learn.memory: RPO = how much data. RTO = how much time.

cards.back: Maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Fully equipped and ready to take over at once.
Space and power only, no ready equipment.
One node works, one waits to take over.

questions.q: A business says it can lose no more than 15 minutes of transactions in a disaster. Which value is being set?
questions.explain: The recovery point objective is about how much data, measured in time, can be lost.

questions.q: The same business must be back online within 4 hours. Which value is this?
questions.explain: The recovery time objective is the maximum time to restore service.

questions.q: A recovery site has racks, power, network links and servers already running with near-live data. What type of site is this?
questions.explain: A hot site can take over almost straight away.

questions.q: Which site is cheapest but takes the longest to bring online?
questions.explain: A cold site is empty space with power and cooling. You bring the hardware.

questions.q: Two firewalls both pass traffic and share the load. If one fails the other carries everything. What is this design?
questions.explain: In active-active both units are live at the same time.

questions.q: Which metric is the average time it takes to fix a failed device?
questions.explain: Mean time to repair measures how quickly you get back up.

questions.q: A small office has one internet connection and one firewall. What is the biggest availability risk?
questions.explain: If either the link or the firewall fails, the whole office is down.

questions.q: The team talks through a ransomware scenario around a table without touching any systems. What kind of test is this?
questions.explain: A tabletop walks through the plan in discussion to find gaps.

questions.q: A differential backup copies everything that changed since the last full backup.
questions.explain: Differentials grow each day until the next full. Incrementals only copy changes since the last backup of any type.

questions.q: Adding a second power supply to a switch removes all single points of failure in the network.
questions.explain: It helps that one switch, but links, other devices and providers can still be single points of failure.

questions.q: Match the term to its meaning.
pairs: How much data loss is acceptable
questions.explain: These four metrics drive DR and availability planning.

questions.q: Which provides redundancy for a server's network connection if one NIC or cable fails?
questions.explain: NIC teaming joins two or more NICs so one can fail without losing the connection.

learn.idea: DHCP hands out addresses, DNS turns names into addresses and NTP keeps clocks in step. When any of them fail, users say the network is down.
points: DHCP DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. A scope holds the address pool, and options give the gateway, DNS servers and more.
Reservations always give the same IP to one MAC. Exclusions keep addresses out of the pool for static devices.
A DHCP relay (IP helper) forwards DHCP broadcasts from a remote subnet to the server.
DNS records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), PTR (reverse lookup), NS (name servers), TXT (text such as SPF), SRV (services), SOA (zone authority).
DNSSEC signs records so clients can check they were not forged. DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS encrypt queries.
A recursive resolver chases the answer for the client. An authoritative server holds the real records for a zone.
NTP uses stratum levels. Stratum 0 is the reference clock, stratum 1 servers connect to it directly. PTP is more precise for things like trading and telecom.
learn.memory: DORA: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

cards.back: One directly connected to a reference clock.

questions.q: Put the DHCP lease process in order.
questions.explain: The client broadcasts Discover, the server offers, the client requests, and the server acknowledges.

questions.q: Users on a new floor subnet get APIPA addresses. The DHCP server is on another subnet and works for everyone else. What is most likely missing?
options: A DHCP relay (IP helper) on the new subnet's router interface
questions.explain: DHCP Discover is a broadcast that routers do not forward. A relay sends it on to the server.

questions.q: A printer must always get 10.1.1.50 from DHCP. What should be configured?
options: A DHCP reservation for its MAC address
questions.explain: A reservation ties one IP to one MAC address.

questions.q: Which DNS record maps a host name to an IPv6 address?
questions.explain: AAAA (quad A) records hold IPv6 addresses. A records hold IPv4.

questions.q: Email for company.com is going nowhere after a DNS change. Which record type should be checked?
questions.explain: MX records tell other mail servers where to deliver mail for the domain.

questions.q: A security tool needs to turn 203.0.113.25 into a host name. Which record is used?
questions.explain: Reverse lookups use PTR records in the in-addr.arpa zone.

questions.q: Which DNS record type is used to publish SPF and domain verification strings?
questions.explain: TXT records hold free text, which SPF, DKIM selectors and verification tokens use.

questions.q: Which feature signs DNS records so a resolver can detect forged answers?
questions.explain: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to records. DoH encrypts queries but does not sign records.

questions.q: Kerberos logons start failing on several servers. Their clocks are 9 minutes apart from the domain controller. What should be fixed?
questions.explain: Kerberos allows only a small clock skew, five minutes by default.

questions.q: Which DNS server type holds the official records for a zone and answers for it directly?
questions.explain: Authoritative servers are the source of truth for their zone.

questions.q: www.example.com should point to the same server as web1.example.com. Which record is best?
questions.explain: A CNAME creates an alias that points one name to another.

questions.q: A DHCP exclusion keeps a range of addresses in the scope from being handed out.
questions.explain: Exclusions protect addresses used by static devices such as servers and printers.

questions.q: PTP is generally less precise than NTP.
questions.explain: Precision Time Protocol reaches sub-microsecond accuracy, far better than NTP.

questions.q: Match the DNS record to what it holds.
pairs: Host and port for a service
questions.explain: Record types are a favourite exam topic.

questions.q: DNS changes made an hour ago are not showing up for some users. What controls how long resolvers keep the old answer?
questions.explain: Resolvers cache records for their time to live. Lowering the TTL before a change speeds things up.

learn.idea: Admins and remote users need safe ways in. VPNs protect user traffic, and out-of-band management keeps a path to devices when the main network is down.
points: Site-to-site VPNs join whole networks. Client-to-site VPNs connect single users.
Full tunnel sends all user traffic through the VPN. Split tunnel only sends company traffic through it.
IPsec uses IKE to set up keys. ESP encrypts and AH only authenticates. Tunnel mode protects the whole packet, transport mode only the payload.
Clientless VPNs work in a browser over TLS.
Manage devices with SSH, HTTPS, or an API. Avoid Telnet and HTTP.
Out-of-band management uses a separate path, such as a console server or cellular modem, to reach gear when production links fail.
A jump box (bastion host) is a hardened server admins connect to first before reaching sensitive systems.
learn.memory: Split tunnel splits the traffic. Full tunnel takes it all home.

cards.back: Full sends all traffic through the VPN. Split sends only company traffic.
A separate path to manage devices when the main network is down.
Hardened host admins use as the only entry to secure systems.
Sets up IPsec security associations and keys.

questions.q: Remote staff should send only company traffic through the VPN and reach the internet directly. Which setting is this?
questions.explain: Split tunnelling sends corporate subnets through the VPN and everything else out the local connection.

questions.q: A security policy says all remote user traffic must pass through the company's web filter. Which VPN setting is required?
questions.explain: A full tunnel sends every packet to the company first.

questions.q: Which IPsec protocol provides encryption?
questions.explain: Encapsulating Security Payload encrypts and authenticates. AH only authenticates.

questions.q: A branch office router must connect permanently to the head office network over the internet. What should be set up?
questions.explain: A site-to-site VPN links two networks through their gateways.

questions.q: A core switch has crashed and taken the management VLAN with it. How can the admin still reach the switch?
options: Through Telnet on the management VLAN
questions.explain: Out-of-band access uses a separate path so it works even when the production network is down.

questions.q: Admins must connect to one hardened server first, which is the only host allowed to SSH to production servers. What is that server?
questions.explain: A jump box or bastion host funnels admin access through one monitored point.

questions.q: Telnet is an acceptable way to manage switches across the company network because it is fast.
questions.explain: Telnet sends passwords and commands in clear text. Use SSH.

questions.q: Match the remote access method to its use.
pairs: Direct local access to a device
questions.explain: Pick the method that is secure and fits the job.

learn.idea: Network security starts with the CIA triad and layers of controls. Authentication proves who you are, authorisation decides what you can do, and accounting records what you did.
points: CIA: confidentiality (only the right people see it), integrity (it was not changed), availability (it is there when needed).
AAA: authentication, authorisation, accounting. RADIUS uses UDP and encrypts only the password. TACACS+ uses TCP 49 and encrypts the whole payload.
MFA combines factors: something you know, have, are, or somewhere you are.
Least privilege gives users only the access they need. Role-based access control assigns rights by job role.
Zero trust means never trust by default, always verify, even inside the network.
Encryption in transit (TLS, IPsec) and at rest (disk encryption). PKI issues certificates that bind public keys to identities.
Segment networks with VLANs, a screened subnet (DMZ) for public servers, and separate networks for IoT and guests.
learn.memory: TACACS+ for admins on TCP. RADIUS for users on UDP.

cards.back: Never trust by default, always verify.

questions.q: Which AAA protocol encrypts the entire payload and is often used for device admin logins?
questions.explain: TACACS+ runs on TCP 49 and encrypts the whole body. RADIUS only hides the password.

questions.q: A hash check shows a firmware file changed after download. Which part of the CIA triad was affected?
questions.explain: Integrity means data has not been altered.

questions.q: A user logs in with a password and then approves a push on their phone. Which factors are used?
options: Something you know and something you have
Something you are and something you know
Somewhere you are and something you have
questions.explain: The password is knowledge and the phone is possession.

questions.q: Where should a company's public web server be placed?
questions.explain: A DMZ separates public facing servers from the internal network.

questions.q: Which principle says users should only get the access needed for their job?
questions.explain: Least privilege limits the damage an account can do.

questions.q: Which model checks the user, device and context for every request, even from inside the office?
questions.explain: Zero trust assumes no request is safe just because of where it comes from.

questions.q: Which part of AAA records what a user did and when?
questions.explain: Accounting logs sessions, commands and usage.

questions.q: RADIUS encrypts the entire packet between the network device and the server.
questions.explain: RADIUS only obfuscates the password field. TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload.

questions.q: IoT devices such as cameras and smart TVs should be placed on their own segmented network.
questions.explain: IoT devices are often weak. Segmentation limits what an attacker can reach through them.

questions.q: Match the access control term to its meaning.
pairs: What you are allowed to do
You cannot deny you did it
questions.explain: These ideas appear in both Network+ and Security+.

questions.q: Which technology issues certificates that bind a public key to a server or user identity?
questions.explain: Public key infrastructure uses certificate authorities to issue and sign certificates.

questions.q: Which RADIUS port is used for authentication?
questions.explain: RADIUS authentication uses UDP 1812 and accounting uses UDP 1813.

questions.q: A firewall placed between the internet and the DMZ, and a second firewall between the DMZ and the LAN, are an example of what?
questions.explain: Layers of controls mean one failure does not expose everything.

questions.q: Data on a stolen laptop's drive cannot be read because the disk is encrypted. Which state of data was protected?
questions.explain: Full disk encryption protects stored data at rest.

learn.idea: Attackers target every layer. On the exam you match the symptoms to the attack and then to the defence.
points: DoS floods one target. DDoS uses many sources, often a botnet. Amplification attacks abuse protocols like DNS or NTP to multiply traffic.
On-path (man-in-the-middle) attacks put the attacker between two hosts. ARP spoofing and rogue DHCP are common ways to do it on a LAN.
VLAN hopping uses switch spoofing (pretending to be a trunk) or double tagging.
MAC flooding fills the switch table so it floods frames like a hub, letting the attacker sniff traffic.
DNS poisoning plants false records. Rogue APs and evil twins trick users into joining fake Wi-Fi.
Social engineering: phishing, tailgating, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving.
Malware includes ransomware, worms, trojans and botnet agents.
learn.memory: Fake gateway MAC in the ARP table? Think ARP spoofing.

cards.back: Fake AP copying a real SSID.
Filling the CAM table so the switch floods traffic.
Denial of service from many sources at once.
Following someone through a secure door.
Clients get a wrong gateway or DNS, enabling on-path attacks.

questions.q: Several PCs suddenly have the default gateway's IP mapped to the MAC address of a user's laptop. Which attack is happening?
questions.explain: ARP spoofing sends fake ARP replies so traffic for the gateway goes to the attacker.

questions.q: A switch's MAC table fills with thousands of random addresses and it starts sending all frames out every port. What attack is this?
questions.explain: Once the CAM table is full the switch floods unknown frames, letting the attacker capture them.

questions.q: A fake access point broadcasts the same SSID as the company network to capture logins. What is it called?
questions.explain: An evil twin copies a trusted SSID so users connect to it.

questions.q: Users get IP addresses with an unknown default gateway after someone plugs a home router into a wall jack. What is this?
questions.explain: The home router is handing out leases. DHCP snooping blocks this.

questions.q: An attacker sends frames with two 802.1Q tags to reach a VLAN they are not on. Which attack is this?
questions.explain: The first switch strips the outer tag, and the inner tag carries the frame into the target VLAN.

questions.q: A web site is knocked offline by traffic from thousands of compromised home devices. What attack is this?
questions.explain: Many sources make it a distributed denial of service, usually driven by a botnet.

questions.q: An attacker spoofs the victim's IP and sends small DNS queries to open resolvers that return huge replies to the victim. What is this?
questions.explain: Amplification multiplies the attacker's traffic using a third party's servers.

questions.q: Someone follows an employee through a badge door without scanning. What is this?
questions.explain: Tailgating or piggybacking defeats access control by walking in behind someone.

questions.q: Users are sent to a fake banking site even though they typed the right URL. Cached DNS answers show the wrong IP. What happened?
questions.explain: Poisoned DNS records point the real name at the attacker's server.

questions.q: Switch spoofing is a VLAN hopping attack where the attacker's device negotiates a trunk with the switch.
questions.explain: If ports auto-negotiate trunking, an attacker can form a trunk and reach every VLAN. Turn off DTP on access ports.

questions.q: A worm needs a user to open a file before it can spread.
questions.explain: Worms spread on their own across the network. A virus needs a host file and user action.

questions.q: Match the attack to its best defence.
pairs: Disable trunk negotiation on access ports
questions.explain: Each Layer 2 attack has a matching switch feature that stops it.

questions.q: A user receives an email that looks like it is from IT asking them to reset their password at a link. What is this?
questions.explain: Phishing uses email. Vishing is voice, smishing is text, and whaling targets executives.

questions.q: An attacker places a device between a user and the file server and relays the traffic while reading it. What is this generally called?
questions.explain: On-path (formerly man-in-the-middle) attacks intercept and may change traffic.

questions.q: Which attack tries every possible password against a login until one works?
questions.explain: Brute force tries all combinations. Lockout policies and MFA defend against it.

questions.q: Ransomware encrypts file shares across the office. Which part of the CIA triad is mainly hit?
questions.explain: The files still exist but nobody can use them. Many ransomware groups also steal data, which hurts confidentiality too.

learn.idea: Hardening shrinks the attack surface. Switch features, ACLs and network access control decide what can connect and what traffic is allowed.
points: Port security limits the MACs allowed on a port. Violation modes are protect, restrict and shutdown (err-disable).
802.1X uses a supplicant (client), authenticator (switch or AP) and authentication server (RADIUS).
DHCP snooping marks trusted ports and blocks DHCP offers from untrusted ones. Dynamic ARP inspection uses the snooping table to drop fake ARP replies.
ACLs filter by source, destination, port and protocol. Rules are read top down and end with an implicit deny.
Change default passwords, disable unused ports and services, use SSH, and keep firmware patched.
Put unused ports in an unused VLAN and shut them down. Change the native VLAN from VLAN 1.
NAC can check device health (patches, antivirus) before giving full access and send failing devices to a remediation VLAN.
learn.memory: ACLs read top down and the last rule you cannot see is deny all.

cards.back: Puts the port in err-disabled state.
Traffic not matched by any ACL rule is dropped.
Shut them down and put them in an unused VLAN.
Checks patches and antivirus before allowing access.

questions.q: A company wants every wired device to authenticate before a switch port will pass traffic. What should be used?
questions.explain: 802.1X holds the port closed until RADIUS approves the device or user.

questions.q: In 802.1X, what role does the switch play?
questions.explain: The switch passes EAP messages between the supplicant and the RADIUS server.

questions.q: An ACL has 'permit tcp any host 10.1.1.10 eq 443' and nothing else. What happens to SSH traffic to 10.1.1.10?
options: It is blocked by the implicit deny
questions.explain: Anything not explicitly permitted hits the hidden deny at the end.

questions.q: A port should only allow the one MAC address of the kiosk PC and disable itself if anything else connects. What should be configured?
options: Port security with a maximum of 1 and shutdown violation mode
questions.explain: Port security with sticky or static MAC and shutdown mode err-disables the port on violation.

questions.q: Which switch feature uses the DHCP snooping table to drop ARP replies that do not match a known IP and MAC pair?
questions.explain: DAI checks every ARP packet on untrusted ports against the binding table.

questions.q: A laptop missing security patches connects and is placed in a limited VLAN with only update servers. What is doing this?
questions.explain: Network access control checks device health and quarantines devices that fail.

questions.q: A user plugs a small switch into an access port and causes a spanning tree change. Which feature would shut that port down when a BPDU arrives?
questions.explain: BPDU guard err-disables access ports that receive BPDUs, which should only come from switches.

questions.q: ACL rules are checked from top to bottom and the first match is applied.
questions.explain: Order matters. Put specific rules above general ones.

questions.q: Leaving unused switch ports enabled in the default VLAN is a good practice because it saves time later.
questions.explain: Unused ports should be shut down and placed in an unused VLAN to stop unauthorised access.

questions.q: Match the 802.1X role to its example.
questions.explain: The authenticator is the middleman between client and server.

questions.q: SIMULATION: Put these ACL lines in the order that blocks one bad host but allows the rest of its subnet to reach the web server.
questions.explain: The specific deny must come first, or the broader permit would match the bad host first. The explicit deny with log at the end records what is dropped.

questions.q: Which is the first hardening step for a brand new switch?
questions.explain: Default credentials are public knowledge and the first thing attackers try.

questions.q: Which switch feature limits how much broadcast or multicast traffic a port may send so a storm cannot swamp the network?
questions.explain: Storm control drops traffic over a set threshold on a port.

questions.q: A firewall rule allows traffic out but must also let the replies back in without a separate inbound rule. What kind of firewall does this?
questions.explain: A stateful firewall tracks connections and lets return traffic through automatically.

questions.q: An admin hid the SSID and turned on MAC filtering to secure the office Wi-Fi. Why is this weak?
options: Free tools reveal hidden SSIDs and attackers can copy an allowed MAC address
MAC filtering slows every client to 11 Mbps
questions.explain: SSIDs still appear in probe and association frames, and MACs are easy to spoof. Use WPA3 and 802.1X instead.

learn.idea: CompTIA uses a seven-step troubleshooting method. Following it in order stops you from making changes before you understand the problem.
points: 1 Identify the problem: gather information, question users, find symptoms, check for recent changes, duplicate the problem, and tackle multiple problems one at a time.
2 Establish a theory of probable cause. Question the obvious. Work top to bottom or bottom to top through the OSI model, or divide and conquer.
3 Test the theory. If it is confirmed, plan the next steps. If not, form a new theory or escalate.
4 Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects.
5 Implement the solution or escalate.
6 Verify full system functionality and put preventive measures in place.
7 Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned.
learn.memory: I Tried To Explain Ideas, Very Dull (Identify, Theory, Test, Establish plan, Implement, Verify, Document).

cards.front: Step after testing a theory that is confirmed?
cards.back: Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects.
Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned.

cards.front: What if the theory is not confirmed?
cards.back: Form a new theory or escalate.

cards.front: When do you put preventive measures in place?

cards.back: Start in the middle of the OSI model and work up or down.

questions.q: Put the CompTIA troubleshooting steps in order.
steps: Establish a theory of probable cause
Test the theory to determine the cause
Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects
Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
Document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned
questions.explain: This is the seven-step method from the Network+ objectives.

questions.q: A technician has confirmed the cause of an outage. What should they do next?
options: Establish a plan of action and identify potential effects
questions.explain: After a theory is confirmed, plan the fix and think about what it might affect.

questions.q: A technician's theory turns out to be wrong. What should happen next?
options: Establish a new theory or escalate
questions.explain: If testing does not confirm the theory, form a new one or escalate.

questions.q: Which action is part of identifying the problem?
questions.explain: Asking what changed is one of the first things to do.

questions.q: A technician starts by checking IP settings and then works up or down depending on what they find. What approach is this?
questions.explain: Divide and conquer starts in the middle of the OSI model.

questions.q: After fixing a problem, the technician makes sure users can work and adds monitoring so it does not happen again. Which step is this?
options: Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
questions.explain: Step 6 confirms the fix works and prevents repeats.

questions.q: A user reports email and web are both down. What is the best first step?
options: Gather information and ask the user questions
questions.explain: Start by identifying the problem. Many issues have simple causes users can describe.

questions.q: Documentation is only needed when a problem had to be escalated.
questions.explain: Every fix should be documented so the next person solves it faster.

questions.q: When users report several problems at once, you should approach them one at a time.
questions.explain: Separating problems avoids mixing up causes and fixes.

questions.q: A technician cannot fix a fault because it is on the ISP's circuit. Which action fits the method?
questions.explain: Escalating is part of steps 3 and 5 when the fix is beyond your control.

learn.idea: Many network faults are physical. Interface counters, link lights and the right tester tell you whether the cable, the port or the settings are at fault.
points: Attenuation is signal loss over distance. Crosstalk is signal bleeding from one pair to another. EMI comes from motors, lights and power cables.
Duplex mismatch: one side full duplex, the other half. Causes late collisions, CRC errors and slow transfers.
Speed mismatch leaves the link down or flapping. Auto-negotiation should match on both ends.
Wrong pinout, such as split pairs, gives poor or no link even if a simple continuity test passes.
Tools: cable tester (wiremap), cable certifier (proves it meets the category), TDR for copper and OTDR for fibre to find breaks, toner and probe, loopback plug, light meter.
Fibre problems: dirty connectors, bent cables past the bend radius, wrong fibre type, or TX and RX swapped.
PoE problems: the device needs more power than the port or switch budget gives.
learn.memory: TDR for copper, OTDR for optical.

cards.front: Tool to find the distance to a break in fibre?
Tool to trace an unlabeled cable?

cards.back: Proves a cable meets its category performance.

cards.front: Fibre link down after install, light present?
cards.back: Check TX/RX are swapped correctly and the fibre type matches.

questions.q: A new fibre link shows no link light. The optics and patch cables are new. What is the most likely cause?
options: Transmit and receive strands are reversed
questions.explain: TX must connect to RX on the far end. Swapping one connector pair usually fixes it.

questions.q: A technician needs to find how far along a buried copper cable a break is. Which tool is used?
questions.explain: A time domain reflectometer measures the reflection from a fault on copper.
