questions.q: Transfers between a server and switch are very slow, and the switch port shows late collisions. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Late collisions are a classic sign that one side is full duplex and the other half.

questions.q: Which tool proves a new cable run meets Cat 6a performance standards for the warranty?
questions.explain: A certifier measures crosstalk, loss and more against the standard.

questions.q: A cable passes a basic continuity test but performs badly with many errors. A certifier shows high crosstalk on two pairs. What is most likely wrong?
options: Split pairs from a bad termination
questions.explain: Split pairs keep continuity but break the twisting that cancels crosstalk.

questions.q: A cable run goes past fluorescent light fittings and a lift motor. Users see lots of errors. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Electromagnetic interference from motors and lights corrupts signals on unshielded cable.

questions.q: A new 802.3bt access point powers on but keeps rebooting. Other APs on the switch are fine. What should be checked?
options: The switch's PoE budget and the port's PoE class
questions.explain: If the switch cannot give the power the AP asks for, the AP may boot loop or run in low-power mode.

questions.q: Which tool tests whether a switch port itself is working, without a cable run?
questions.explain: A loopback plug feeds the port's transmit back to its receive.

questions.q: A Cat 6 run of 130 m may link up but is likely to have errors because of attenuation.
questions.explain: Past 100 m the signal weakens too much for reliable Ethernet.

questions.q: An OTDR is the right tool for finding a fault in a copper patch cable.
questions.explain: OTDRs are for fibre. Use a TDR or cable tester for copper.

questions.q: Match the symptom to its likely cause.
pairs: CRC errors on a long run near machinery
No light on a new fibre link
questions.explain: Linking symptoms to causes is the core of troubleshooting questions.

questions.q: A fibre patch cable was pulled tight around a sharp rack edge and now has high loss. What was exceeded?
questions.explain: Bending fibre too tightly lets light leak out and raises loss.

learn.idea: When the cable is fine, look at addressing, switching and routing. Most of these faults show up as some hosts working and others not.
points: Wrong subnet mask or gateway: the host can reach some local hosts but not other networks.
Duplicate IP addresses cause warnings and intermittent loss. Duplicate MACs are rare and usually point to cloning or spoofing.
DHCP scope exhaustion: new devices get APIPA addresses while old ones keep working.
Wrong VLAN on a port: the device gets an address from the wrong subnet or none at all.
Routing loops cause TTL exceeded messages. Missing routes cause destination unreachable.
Switching loops cause broadcast storms and MAC flapping. STP misconfiguration can leave ports blocked or unblocked wrongly.
Asymmetric routing sends replies down a different path, which stateful firewalls may drop. Incorrect ACLs block the traffic they were meant to allow.
learn.memory: Some hosts fine, new ones on APIPA? Check if the DHCP scope is full.

cards.back: Local works, remote networks do not.
The same MAC appears on different ports quickly, often from a loop.
A stateful firewall drops replies it did not see leave.

questions.q: New laptops in a conference room get 169.254 addresses, but desktops that have been on all day work fine. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Old devices keep their leases. New ones cannot get one because the pool is full. Shorten the lease or grow the scope.

questions.q: A host can ping devices on its own subnet but nothing on other subnets. Other hosts on the subnet are fine. What should be checked first?
questions.explain: Off-subnet traffic goes to the gateway. A wrong or missing gateway breaks only remote access.

questions.q: A traceroute shows the same two routers repeating until the trace hits 30 hops. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Packets bounce between routers until the TTL runs out.

questions.q: Two users get 'IP address conflict' messages every morning. What is the likely cause?
options: A static IP was set inside the DHCP pool
questions.explain: A static address inside the scope can be leased to another device too. Use exclusions or reservations.

questions.q: A switch log shows one MAC address moving between Gi1/0/3 and Gi1/0/9 many times a second, and the network is crawling. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: MAC flapping with heavy slowdown points to a Layer 2 loop and broadcast storm.

questions.q: A PC in the finance office receives an address from the guest subnet. What is most likely wrong?
options: The switch port is in the wrong VLAN
The PC's DNS cache is old
questions.explain: The VLAN on the port decides which subnet and DHCP scope the device lands in.

questions.q: A host is set to 192.168.1.50 with mask 255.255.0.0 while everyone else uses 255.255.255.0. What is the likely symptom?
options: It cannot reach some remote 192.168.x.x subnets because it thinks they are local
It cannot reach anything at all
questions.explain: A too-large mask makes the host ARP for addresses that are really behind the router.

questions.q: A firewall drops return traffic for some connections after a second ISP link was added. Traffic leaves on one link and returns on the other. What is this?
questions.explain: A stateful firewall only knows the session it saw leave, so replies arriving on another path look unsolicited.

questions.q: Users on VLAN 40 cannot reach the server VLAN since a new ACL was applied. Other VLANs are fine. What should be checked?
options: The ACL rules and their order on the VLAN 40 interface
questions.explain: A wrong or misordered ACL entry can block traffic you meant to allow.

questions.q: A ping reply of 'Destination host unreachable' from a router means the router has no route or no ARP answer for the destination.
questions.explain: The router is telling you it cannot deliver the packet any further.

questions.q: If one PC on a subnet cannot reach the internet but all others can, the ISP circuit is the most likely cause.
questions.explain: When only one host fails, look at that host first: its settings, cable and port.

questions.q: Match the symptom to the cause.
pairs: Local OK, remote fails for one host
questions.explain: Each symptom points to a different layer and fix.

questions.q: A switch port connected to another switch shows as blocking in STP and users downstream are cut off. The redundant link was removed last week. What should be done?
options: Check STP settings and port roles since the topology changed
questions.explain: If STP did not reconverge or a port is set wrongly, it can stay blocked even with no loop left.

questions.q: Which command on a Windows PC shows whether its address came from DHCP and when the lease ends?
questions.explain: ipconfig /all lists DHCP Enabled, the DHCP server, and lease obtained and expires times.

questions.intro: Ticket #5110: 'No internet since this morning.' Other users on the same floor are fine. The cable was swapped by facilities yesterday.

learn.idea: Slow is a problem too. Latency, jitter, packet loss and congestion hurt voice and video first. Wireless adds interference, coverage and roaming issues.
points: Latency is delay. Jitter is variation in delay. Packet loss is packets that never arrive. Voice wants under 150 ms one way, under 30 ms jitter and under 1% loss.
Congestion and bottlenecks happen where traffic from fast links squeezes into a slower one.
QoS uses classification and marking (DSCP, CoS) and queuing to give voice and video priority.
Wireless issues: interference, channel overlap, low signal (RSSI), poor SNR, too many clients per AP, roaming problems, and wrong antenna placement.
Microwave ovens, Bluetooth and cordless phones interfere with 2.4 GHz.
An AP with power set too high can make clients cling to it while far away (sticky clients).
Use a Wi-Fi analyser to see channels and signal, and a spectrum analyser to find non-Wi-Fi interference.
learn.memory: Latency is the wait. Jitter is the wobble in the wait.

cards.front: Max one-way latency for good voice?

cards.back: Client stays on a far AP instead of roaming to a closer one.

questions.q: VoIP calls sound choppy, with words cut out, but web browsing is fine. Monitoring shows delay varying from 20 ms to 180 ms. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Jitter is the variation in delay. Voice needs a steady stream of packets.

questions.q: Which technology gives voice traffic priority over file downloads on a busy WAN link?
questions.explain: Quality of service marks and queues traffic so voice goes first.

questions.q: Wi-Fi in the break room drops every lunchtime. Which tool would best show the cause?
questions.explain: A spectrum analyser reveals non-Wi-Fi interference such as microwave ovens on 2.4 GHz.

questions.q: Laptops stay connected to an AP at the far end of the hall with a weak signal instead of the AP next to them. What is the likely cause?
options: AP transmit power is set too high, causing sticky clients
The DHCP lease is too long
questions.explain: Lowering power on the APs helps clients roam to the closest one.

questions.q: A wireless survey shows two neighbouring APs both on 2.4 GHz channel 6 and users near both have slow speeds. What should be done?
options: Move one AP to channel 1 or 11
questions.explain: Co-channel interference makes APs share airtime. Use 1, 6 and 11 so neighbours differ.

questions.q: Users in a 300-seat lecture hall connect but speeds are very poor when the hall is full. What is the likely cause?
questions.explain: Each AP shares airtime among all its clients. Dense areas need more APs on more channels.

questions.q: Which value measures received Wi-Fi signal strength in dBm?
questions.explain: RSSI is the received signal strength. -67 dBm or better is a common target for voice.

questions.q: A signal of -85 dBm is stronger than -55 dBm.
questions.explain: dBm values are negative and closer to zero is stronger. -55 dBm is much stronger.

questions.q: Packet loss above a few percent can make video calls freeze even when bandwidth is high.
questions.explain: Lost packets cannot be replaced in time for live media, so frames drop.

questions.q: A 1 Gbps LAN feeds a 100 Mbps WAN link and users see drops and slow transfers at peak times. Where is the problem?
options: A bottleneck where fast traffic squeezes into the slower WAN link
A duplex mismatch on every PC
questions.explain: Traffic queues and drops where a fast network meets a slower link. QoS, more bandwidth or traffic shaping help.

questions.q: Which Layer 3 QoS field marks a packet's priority so routers can queue voice ahead of bulk data?
questions.explain: Differentiated Services Code Point bits in the IP header carry the class. EF (46) is the usual value for voice.

learn.idea: Command-line tools tell you what the network is doing right now. On the exam and in these labs you pick the right command for the job and read its output.
points: ping tests reachability with ICMP. tracert (Windows) and traceroute (Linux) show each hop. pathping combines both and measures loss per hop.
ipconfig /all (Windows) and ip a (Linux) show addresses, MAC, gateway and DNS. ipconfig /release, /renew and /flushdns fix common client issues.
arp -a shows the ARP cache. Linux uses ip neigh or arp -n. The cache only fills after the host talks to a device.
nslookup and dig test DNS. netstat or ss show open ports and connections. nmap scans hosts and ports.
show interfaces, show mac address-table, show vlan brief, show ip route and show running-config are key switch and router commands.
tcpdump and Wireshark capture packets. iperf measures throughput between two hosts.
LLDP and CDP let devices discover their neighbours. show lldp neighbors tells you what is on the other end of a cable.
learn.memory: Ping says if. Tracert says where.

questions.explain: ip a (ip address) lists interfaces and their addresses.

questions.q: A technician wants to know the real throughput between two offices across a new WAN link. Which tool should be used?
questions.explain: iperf pushes traffic between a client and server and reports throughput.

questions.q: Which command queries DNS for a domain's MX records on Linux?
questions.explain: dig lets you choose the record type to query.

questions.q: Which command line tool can find which hosts are up on a subnet and what ports they have open?

questions.q: On a Linux host, which command shows the ARP (neighbour) table?

questions.q: arp -a will list every device on the subnet even if the PC has never communicated with them.
questions.explain: The ARP cache only holds addresses the host has resolved recently. Ping or scan first to fill it.
